title: The Festival That Wasn’t There
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 17 of 40
content:
Aang woke us before sunrise by ringing a bell in the courtyard.

Toph threw a pillow through the window.

The bell stopped.

Aang leaned around the doorframe five seconds later, hair windblown and expression deeply offended.

“That was a ceremonial bell.”

“It was a loud ceremonial bell.”

“It belonged to the Eastern Air Temple.”

Toph sat upright in bed. “Then why was it in my courtyard?”

“Our courtyard,” Katara mumbled into the pillow beside her.

Toph pointed toward the sound of her voice. “Traitor.”

I opened one eye. “Why are we awake?”

Aang brightened.

That was never a good sign before dawn.

“Yangchen’s Festival.”

Toph fell backward.

Katara pushed herself up on one elbow. “Today?”

“Traditionally, yes.”

“You said next week.”

“I was wrong.”

Toph’s voice came muffled through the blanket. “Avatar wisdom.”

By breakfast, the house was full of strings, cloth, prayer wheels, flour, fruit, and three Air Acolytes who had arrived carrying a crate of things Aang insisted were not decorations.

“They have symbolic purpose.”

“They’re ribbons,” Toph said.

“They can be both.”

The festival had not been celebrated properly in more than a century.

That fact lived underneath everything Aang did that morning.

He smiled. He gave instructions. He tied colored strips of cloth from the roofline and corrected an Acolyte’s pronunciation gently enough that the young man did not notice he had been corrected at all.

But every few minutes Aang stopped.

His hand would rest on some ordinary object—a carved bowl, a length of saffron cloth, a bundle of incense—and his expression would go distant.

Memory without memory.

That was one of the cruelest things about what had been taken from him. He could remember his people. He could remember individual monks, games, rules he broke, meals he hated, the way certain halls smelled when it rained.

But he had been twelve.

There were ceremonies he had watched without learning. Songs he knew only in fragments. Customs adults would have explained later, if later had happened.

Now people looked at him as if being the last Air Nomad meant he must also be the complete archive of them.

At midmorning, he handed me a stack of copied festival notes.

“Can you organize these?”

I flipped through them. “By what?”

Aang frowned.

“Exactly.”

Half came from his own memory. Some had been copied from temple records. Others came from old Earth Kingdom travel diaries written by visitors who had watched Air Nomad festivals from outside and misunderstood half of what they saw.

One paper claimed the holiday required floating three onions down a river.

Aang stared at it.

“I have never heard of that.”

Toph took the page. “Keep it.”

“No.”

“Coward.”

Katara carried trays of dough into the courtyard. “What did the festival actually celebrate?”

Aang’s face softened.

“Gratitude. Letting go of what we don’t need. Remembering that everything changes.”

Toph bit into a piece of uncooked dough.

Katara slapped her hand away.

“That part seems useful,” I said.

Aang looked toward the street beyond the gate.

The city had changed even in the months I had known it. New smokestacks interrupted the horizon. Construction cranes turned above old tile roofs. People from every nation filled streets that had once belonged to one empire or another.

“Yeah,” he said. “It does.”

We held the festival at the edge of town, on a low hill where an abandoned Air Nomad waystation had once stood.

Only the foundation remained.

Aang had found it in an old map and spent weeks getting the council to protect the site from a factory expansion. Toph said the stones were still good. Katara found a spring nearby and cleared the channel until water ran again.

I made signs explaining that visitors should not climb on the ruin.

Nobody read them.

Before the gathering began, an elderly neighbor asked whether the ribbons were supposed to carry the names of the dead. Aang hesitated. He had imagined releasing burdens, not creating a memorial roll.
"I should have explained," he said.
"You explained what it means to you," Katara replied. "They may need something different."
Toph planted a heel in the dirt. "Also, your writing table is crooked. The left leg sank."
She lifted the ground beneath it just enough to level the brushes. Aang set blank paper beside the instructions.
"I can't claim this is exactly how my people celebrated," he told the first guests. "Some of it I remember. Some of it we're making together. You can write, draw, or leave the paper empty."
One person wrote a brother's name. A child drew a tree.
Katara checked where the loose ribbons would land. "We have to collect the ones that fall into the stream. I don't want somebody else's water spoiled by our ceremony."
"I can help them rise," Aang said.
"And I can make sure they don't stay in the creek."
Toph brought four cups of water. "And I can make sure you noble idiots drink something."
When I laughed, she bumped my shoulder. The festival was imperfect. It was better than pretending history had left us flawless directions.

The gathering grew larger than expected.

Air Acolytes came in gray and yellow robes. Local families arrived out of curiosity. Children chased paper gliders down the hill. Vendors appeared because vendors could smell a crowd across three districts.

Aang tried to object to the fried-dough cart.

Then he ate two.

At noon, he stood on the old foundation and spoke.

Not as the Avatar.

As Aang.

“This used to be a small stop for travelers,” he said. “Not a temple. Not a sacred place because somebody important lived here. Sacred because people rested here. Shared food. Told stories. Then moved on.”

The crowd quieted.

He held one of the copied pages in his hand.

“I don’t know everything about this festival.”

A few Acolytes looked surprised.

Aang smiled a little.

“I know some things. I remember some. I’ve learned others from records. And some things are gone.”

The last word landed harder than the rest.

Katara moved closer to him.

Toph stayed where she was, feet planted on the stone.

Aang continued. “If we pretend I remember what I don’t, then we aren’t preserving Air Nomad culture. We’re inventing certainty because grief makes uncertainty uncomfortable.”

I looked at him and felt my throat tighten.

“That doesn’t mean we do nothing,” he said. “It means we practice honestly. We say what we know. We say what we don’t. We keep the values that mattered: compassion, freedom, joy, nonviolence, care for all life. And we let living people learn how to carry them forward.”

The wind rose as he spoke, tugging at ribbons overhead.

For one breath, the hill seemed crowded with ghosts.

Not visible.

Not supernatural.

Just present in the space Aang made for them without pretending they could answer every question.

Later, we tied written burdens to thin paper streamers and let them go from the ridge.

Not an exact historical ritual, Aang warned everyone.

“A new one,” he said.

Toph held her paper for a long time.

“What’d you write?” I asked.

“None of your business.”

“Fair.”

She crumpled it.

Then smoothed it again.

Aang stood several paces away helping a child fold a glider. Katara was laughing with an elderly woman who had mistaken rice flour for face powder and somehow covered both of them in white dust.

Toph angled her head toward me.

“You?”

I looked down at my own strip.

I had written: THE FEAR THAT I AM BORROWING SOMEONE ELSE’S FAMILY.

“Also none of your business.”

“Good answer.”

We walked to the ridge together.

Toph did not need to see the horizon to know where the wind was coming from. She lifted her paper and waited until the current pulled against it.

“On three?” I asked.

“No.”

She let go immediately.

I laughed and released mine after hers.

The papers spun upward.

Toph could not follow them with her eyes.

I almost described it.

Then I stopped myself.

“Want to know?”

Her mouth tilted.

“Yeah.”

“Yours got caught in an updraft. Mine’s losing a fight with a tree.”

“Sounds right.”

Aang came up behind us.

“Toph, did you actually write something?”

“No.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“I’m the best liar. I can tell when everybody else is doing it.”

“That is not how that works.”

Katara joined us and slipped an arm around my waist.

“What did you write?” I asked her.

She looked toward the streamers.

“That I don’t have to keep every version of home exactly the way I remember it.”

Aang turned toward her.

Katara gave him a small smile.

“The South is changing. This city is changing. We’re changing.”

Toph made a gagging noise.

Katara leaned over and kissed her cheek.

Toph froze.

Then, very deliberately, wiped her cheek on my shoulder.

“Gross.”

“You’re blushing,” Aang said.

“I will bury you in this sacred historical site.”

“You can’t. Paperwork put up a sign.”

I pointed downhill. “Finally, respect for municipal authority.”

That evening, after the crowd left, we stayed to clean.

The hill was littered with cups, snapped strings, crumbs, and the evidence of three hundred people attempting spirituality near food vendors.

Aang swept with a broom instead of bending.

I asked why.

He shrugged. “Monks made us clean after festivals.”

“Tradition?”

“Punishment.”

“For what?”

“Being children near a festival.”

I laughed.

He leaned on the broom.

“Was it wrong?” he asked.

I knew what he meant.

The new ritual. The things he had filled in. The celebration built partly from memory and partly from choice.

“No.”

“You don’t know that.”

“No,” I said. “I know you told the truth about what you knew. You didn’t ask anyone to confuse invention with history.”

His gaze dropped.

“And it made people care enough to learn more.”

Aang looked across the hill where an Air Acolyte carefully wrapped an old stone marker before carrying it indoors for preservation.

The wind moved through his robes.

“Maybe that’s enough for now.”

“Maybe ‘for now’ is allowed.”

He smiled.

Then he hooked the broom behind my knees with airbending and almost knocked me into a basket.

I stared at him.

“Sacred tradition?”

“Extremely.”

I chased the Avatar down the hill while Toph shouted unhelpful tactical advice and Katara laughed hard enough to drop the trash bag.

Behind us, new ribbons snapped in the evening wind above old stones.

Not restoration.

Not replacement.

Something living.
